text: Quantum gates are matrices, quantum states are vectors, and applying a gate is just matrix-vector multiplication. This lesson covers the small set of NumPy operations that make up essentially all the math in quantum computing code.

The at-sign operator performs real matrix multiplication, while the star operator multiplies element by element. Applying a gate to a state is gate at-sign state, matrix-vector multiplication. Quantum mechanics constantly needs the conjugate transpose, written U dagger, which NumPy builds by chaining dot-conj and dot-T. And np dot dot tells you whether two state vectors are orthogonal, meaning perfectly distinguishable by measurement.

This is the single most important distinction in this lesson. H star H just squares each entry, point five everywhere, which isn't useful here. H at-sign H performs the real matrix product and gives back the identity matrix, confirming that applying the Hadamard gate twice does nothing at all — it's its own inverse.

Applying at-sign between a matrix and a vector is literally what applying a gate means in code. Pauli-X at-sign the state zero gives one, flipping the basis vector exactly as expected. Hadamard at-sign the state zero gives point seven zero seven one and point seven zero seven one, the equal-superposition plus state every quantum algorithm starts a qubit in.

Pauli-Y has genuinely imaginary entries, a good test of conj. Transposing Y and then conjugating every entry reconstructs Y itself exactly, which means Y is Hermitian, equal to its own conjugate transpose, a property every valid quantum observable shares.
Next lesson connects this math to measurement: why every eigenvalue numpy dot linalg dot eig computes from a gate matrix is a real, physically possible measurement outcome.
